To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the addition of 2,000 non‐prostate cancer‐associated variants to the existing polygenic risk score improves prediction of prostate cancer risk in the discovery and replication datasets and 2) the polygenic risk score based on 2,000 variants has a similar predictive performance in men of different ancestry.
a polygenic risk score including all known prostate cancer genetic variants can be used to predict the genetic risk of prostate cancer in individual men.

1) a polygenic risk score comprising established prostate cancer risk variants is an informative predictor of prostate cancer risk in men of European descent; 2) inclusion of genetic variants with moderate effect sizes, not reaching genome‐wide significance, improves the performance of polygenic risk score for prediction of prostate cancer risk; 3) a polygenic score comprising established prostate and non‐prostate cancer risk variants is a more powerful predictor of prostate cancer compared with a polygenic score including only prostate cancer risk
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of polygenic risk scores for the prediction of prostate cancer.
the identification and characterisation of genetic variants that influence susceptibility to prostate cancer.
the development of a polygenic score to predict individual genetic risk to develop prostate cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current polygenic risk score for prostate cancer is a useful tool to predict individual genetic risk for the disease and may have a role in clinical decision‐making.
the polygenic score for prostate cancer risk is informative for prostate cancer prediction, however, it is not sufficiently predictive to replace clinical decision making.
a genetic risk score based on established susceptibility variants is an informative classifier of prostate cancer risk.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inclusion of additional genetic markers that are not genome‐wide significant does not improve disease prediction.
we have identified a number of new genetic markers for prostate cancer, and that these markers improve the ability to predict prostate cancer in men of European ancestry.

polygenic risk score (PRS) based on the 94 prostate cancer risk variants (including 2 variants with a p‐value of 1.00×10−6) identified by the PRACTICAL consortium is a better predictor for prostate cancer risk than PRS comprising only the 17 prostate cancer variants identified at genome‐wide significant (p<5×10−8) level by the PRACTICAl consortium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
inclusion of additional risk loci that are not genome‐wide significant can improve prediction of genetic risk to prostate cancers, particularly in men at high risk of the disease.
inclusion of genetic variants that are associated with prostate cancer but not at a genome‐wise significance level can improve prediction of prostate cancer.

a polygenic risk score comprising established susceptibility variants is informative for prostate cancer risk, but that the inclusion of additional genetic variants that have not been associated with the disease does not improve the prediction.
